> We could still use Vector with resize, and then get the ptr, and fill it _manually_, which involve keeping indexes for each one, but it avoids the last copies. This is definitely harder to write and more error prone, so this version is a good trade off. 

I started with that approach, but indeed, the code was more intrusive, error prone, and provided no performance benefit.

> ... and provided no performance benefit.

It had a small but noticeable difference before hence why we have a lot of older code like that but ever since `LocalVector::push_back()` was changed to use `std:move` the `push_back()` of an already allocated LocalVector costs near nothing. Might no longer be worth it anymore in some cases to run with resize + index for all that added code complexity. Meanwhile a resized Vector still does a lot of its CowData and ref related check shenanigans , just not a full copy, so it could still be a little slower in comparison even with ptrw() but it would avoid a copy at the end. In case of mesh arrays it does not really matter because it will make a copy anyway.

> > We could still use Vector with resize, and then get the ptr, and fill it manually, which involve keeping indexes for each one, but it avoids the last copies. This is definitely harder to write and more error prone, so this version is a good trade off.
> 
> It is in general a bit faster, but won't be much for a relatively small amount of points, and I guess not worth the effort.
> 
> A quick synthetic test
> Vector::push_back 22786 ms LocalVector::push_back 3144 ms Vector::ptrw 2230 ms

Definitely not the same magnitude as the first improvement for sure, but that is not nothing. May be worth it for the types that are commonly used.

> > We could still use Vector with resize, and then get the ptr, and fill it manually, which involve keeping indexes for each one, but it avoids the last copies. This is definitely harder to write and more error prone, so this version is a good trade off.
> 
> It is in general a bit faster, but won't be much for a relatively small amount of points, and I guess not worth the effort.
> 
> A quick synthetic test
> Vector::push_back 22786 ms LocalVector::push_back 3144 ms Vector::ptrw 2230 ms

That's not an apples to apples comparison. The compiler will fully vectorize your loop in this case (when not using push back). But it can't vectorize the loop in practice for PrimitiveMeshes. 

I profiled the actual performance benefit and there was none. A synthetic benchmark is no replacement for the real thing.

Also, the cost of the type conversion from LocalVector to Vector is also negligible, in the profiler it is <1% of the overall cost of the function. It's really not worth trying to optimize. 

The only things left that would make a measurable impact are:
1. Caching the calls to sin/cos/sqrt since they are responsible for the vast majority of the cost of this function
2. Restructure the loops entirely and use templating to allow the compiler to auto-vectorize. 

Both changes would require a total refactor _and_ have an upper limit of benefit that is less than this relatively simple change. It's just not worth it

> Definitely not the same magnitude as the first improvement for sure, but that is not nothing. May be worth it for the types that are commonly used.

It will be much smaller in a real case (relative to the rest of the function), all difference is from `LocalVector::push_back` extra weight. It's only noticeable if you have a lot of points. And the last copy seems to be pretty much negated by larger `Vector::resize` weight.

> The compiler will fully vectorize your loop in this case (when not using push back).

Numbers are from debug build with most optimizations disabled, including `-fno-vectorize`. But it's not representative regardless of this.
